      <description><p>Committee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza</p><p></p><p>The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/sep/16/israel-committed-genocide-in-gaza-says-un-inquiry">that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza</a>.</p><p>The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/09/navanethem-navi-pillay-wins-nobel-peace-prize">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Isaias strengthens to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 season</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/09/isaias-strengthens-first-atlantic-hurricane-2026</link>
      <description><p>Storm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river flooding</p><p>Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).</p><p>As a result of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/sep/26/what-is-el-nino-causes-can-we-reduce-risks">the strong El Niño</a>, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/09/isaias-strengthens-first-atlantic-hurricane-2026">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2026/oct/09/egypt-six-journalists-matsadaash-protest-over-detentions</link>
      <description><p>Matsadaash staff allege torture and forced confessions after being held on charges of working for Muslim Brotherhood</p><p>Egyptian journalists are planning a new protest in Cairo this weekend after <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/04/egyptian-journalist-faces-terrorism-charges-entire-newsroom-detained-matsadaash-press-freedom">six colleagues were charged with terrorism offences</a> amid allegations they had been tortured in police detention.</p><p>Last week, Egyptian authorities arrested the journalists, from the independent factchecking and investigative platform Matsadaash, accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and producing false news on behalf of the outlawed <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/muslim-brotherhood">Muslim Brotherhood</a>.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2026/oct/09/egypt-six-journalists-matsadaash-protest-over-detentions">Continue reading...</a></description>

News from the US, Europe, Asia Pacific, Africa, Middle East, America</description><link>https://www.france24.com/en/</link><lastBuildDate>Tue, 13 Oct 2026 11:20:48 GMT</lastBuildDate><atom:link href="https://www.france24.com/en/rss" rel="self" type="application/rss+xml"/><item><category></category><title>Hackers heat French supermarket fridges, sparking fires and spoiling food</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261013-hackers-heat-french-supermarket-fridges-sparking-fires-and-spoiling-food</link><description>
Major French supermarket chains on Monday said they were hit by a cyberattack that caused their refrigerators to shoot up in temperature in hundreds of stores, forcing spoiled food to be thrown away and raising concerns about food security.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/3fab756c-c6f6-11f1-b375-3774aeac812a/w:1024/p:16x9/mini-36.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/3fab756c-c6f6-11f1-b375-3774aeac812a/w:1024/p:16x9/mini-36.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">4fb384cc-c6f6-11f1-8a7f-854631bc0e37</guid><pubDate>Tue, 13 Oct 2026 11:13:14 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>India’s youth-led Cockroach movement defies protest ban</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/india-s-youth-led-cockroach-movement-defies-protest-ban</link><description>
India’s youth-led Cockroach movement is intensifying protests against Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government. Three leaders were detained after defying a ban at New Delhi’s Jantar Mantar protest site. Demonstrators are challenging a voter-list revision they claim favours Modi’s party, while the protests disrupt businesses across the capital.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/4b962c40-c6f2-11f1-b580-3774aeac812a/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261013-120704-120853-CS.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/4b962c40-c6f2-11f1-b580-3774aeac812a/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261013-120704-120853-CS.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">50936e10-c6f2-11f1-8188-45191249cb5c</guid><pubDate>Tue, 13 Oct 2026 11:00:18 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category>Press Review</category><title>The Times: How Infantino's 'second salary' paid for luxury life in Miami</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/press-review/20261013-the-times-how-infantino-s-second-salary-paid-for-luxury-life-in-miami</link><description>
PRESS REVIEW – Tuesday, October 13: "Act 5" of the French high school protest movement begins as teachers and farmers could join in too. In India, thousands of opposition supporters have marched to the Supreme Court demanding the resignation of the electoral board chief over fraud allegations. The Times of London publishes an investigation that shows FIFA boss Gianni Infantino received a second, undeclared salary. Finally, a cat in China goes viral with people flocking from around the world to meet her.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/275aac9e-c6d3-11f1-b94b-e362370cce2e/w:1024/p:16x9/Anglais-2026-10-13T05-25-23-994Z.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/275aac9e-c6d3-11f1-b94b-e362370cce2e/w:1024/p:16x9/Anglais-2026-10-13T05-25-23-994Z.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">2d1acbaa-c6d3-11f1-b4e1-e972af3c3bd1</guid><pubDate>Tue, 13 Oct 2026 10:59:23 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>Dheepthika LAURENT</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>France: climate activist Greta Thunberg joins teens on new day of school protests</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/france-climate-activist-greta-thunberg-joins-teens-on-new-day-of-school-protests</link><description>
French students are taking to the streets for a fourth consecutive week of protests over poor school conditions, including teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and deteriorating facilities. Backed by trade unions and university students, the movement has led to school blockades and clashes with police. Swedish activist Greta Thunberg joined a demonstration near Paris, while around 200 schools were reported closed amid the mobilisation. FRANCE 24's Clovis Casali has the latest from the ground.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/1361e236-c6e0-11f1-8b8b-3774aeac812a/w:1024/p:16x9/000-D33G87T.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/1361e236-c6e0-11f1-8b8b-3774aeac812a/w:1024/p:16x9/000-D33G87T.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">319f33a0-c6f1-11f1-a703-ed43eedad4aa</guid><pubDate>Tue, 13 Oct 2026 10:40:53 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>US economists win Nobel for research helping policymakers navigate crises</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/us-economists-win-nobel-for-research-helping-policymakers-navigate-crises</link><description>
Two American economists, Robert E. Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University, have won the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for their work on economic stabilisation. Their research helps policymakers and central banks better understand economic fluctuations, manage recessions and inflation, and account for public expectations when shaping economic policy. The prize money, worth around $1.2 million, will be shared equally between the two laureates.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/81e7cf3c-c6e9-11f1-9fbf-29a2e29ae696/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261013-111231-111403-CS.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/81e7cf3c-c6e9-11f1-9fbf-29a2e29ae696/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261013-111231-111403-CS.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">86fcb47e-c6e9-11f1-933e-7d8170ba1900</guid><pubDate>Tue, 13 Oct 2026 10:04:59 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item></channel></rss>

<![CDATA[ Latest from Space.com ]]> https://www.space.com/feeds.xml Tue, 13 Oct 2026 12:00:00 +0000 en <![CDATA[ The great Halley's Comet disappointment of 1986 — and the discoveries that changed astronomy forever ]]> This year, 2026, marks the 40th anniversary of the most recent appearance of Halley's Comet, the most famous comet in the solar system.

Roughly every 76 years, Halley punctuates history like an exclamation mark in the night sky. As writer Guy Ottewell has said, it is the "wildest of the tame comets."

It is a tame comet because it can be anticipated. It is wild because it is still fresh and bright; the brightest of all the recurring comets. It is the only one that periodically becomes conspicuous to the naked eye.

Halley through history

Before 1986, Halley had been seen and recorded on 29 occasions. In A.D. 66, observers described it as a sword in the skies above Jerusalem. In 1066, its image was woven into the strip of linen now known as the Bayeux Tapestry, where an agitated crowd of Saxons points toward a fiery comet we know to be Halley. In 1301, the Florentine painter Giotto di Bondone witnessed the comet and was so impressed that, a few years later, he depicted a comet as the star that led the Magi to Bethlehem in one of his magnificent frescoes in Padua's Scrovegni Chapel.

More recently, Halley passed unusually close to Earth in 1910. As the 1986 return approached, people who remembered that earlier appearance likely told their children and grandchildren about being awakened before dawn and taken outside to see a huge, ghostly, gleaming object in the sky.

Halley's earlier appearances suggested that each return to the inner solar system might produce a magnificent display. Little wonder, then, that the public expected great things in 1986.

The great disappointment of 1986

Halley's 1986 return therefore became two very different stories: a frustrating spectacle for much of the public and an unprecedented scientific opportunity for astronomers.

But for many who saw it — or tried to — in 1986, Halley is remembered as a tremendous disappointment. Heavily promoted as the most anticipated celestial event of the second half of the 20th century, the comet proved to be an underwhelming sight that belied promises of a spectacle never to be seen again.

In all fairness, Halley's subpar performance was not unexpected. During the mid-1970's, comet experts had warned that the comet would likely disappoint much of the general public. Despite that, the comet's impending arrival was accompanied by a frenzy of T-shirts, commemorative comet medals, bumper stickers, and specially marketed telescopes. Halley logos could be found on warm-up jackets, cocktail glasses, cereal boxes, and just about everything in sight. Caught up in the grip of Halley-mania, the mainstream media emphasized that the comet would be a "once-in-a-lifetime spectacle."

One of the main problems for many trying to see the comet that year was light pollution; the total outdoor illumination in the United States had increased tremendously since Halley's previous visit in 1910. Indeed, in 1986, many of the largest cities were bathed in permanent twilight, with only the brightest stars and planets visible from near city centers and with astronomically unacceptable conditions up to 50 miles (80 km) away.

On the evening of Jan. 11, in New York City, thousands gathered at four city parks to get a view of Halley's Comet. Mayor Ed Koch and Parks Commissioner Henry J. Stern arranged to have the lights turned off at four public parks, where telescopes were set up. The comet itself was not overly impressive, but many were still happy just to get a glimpse of it. As Stern put it: "Those who came for the comet saw the comet — the cynics didn't — but it was there."

When Halley passed through perihelion — its closest point to the sun — on Feb. 9, it lay on the far side of the sun as viewed from Earth and was hidden in the solar glare. During much of March, it brightened only to third magnitude and displayed a tail about a dozen degrees long, merely one-tenth the extent of its 1910 splendor. At the same time, it moved southward through the stars of Sagittarius, Scorpius, and Centaurus. Because those constellations appear low above the southern horizon, the comet was difficult to see from Canada, Europe, and the northern United States.

The 1986 apparition was, in fact, described as the comet's worst in 2,000 years. And as one would expect, the public wasn't impressed. Having read that he'd need binoculars and a star map just to find the comet, taxi driver David A. Gittelman penned a New York Times opinion piece entitled "Who Cares About Halley's Comet Anyway?" In it he wrote:

"I was devastated. How could such an injustice be allowed to prevail? All my life I'd been waiting — all my life. What happened to the cosmic leviathan of my childhood dreams?"

What happened was that at its closest approach to Earth on April 10, Halley was nearly three times farther away than at its minimum distance in 1910. And it had arrived at this point a full two months after perihelion (instead of two weeks as in 1910) — long after its brightest phase had passed. Even those living or traveling to the Southern Hemisphere (as I did), where the comet was well placed, didn't witness a true showstopper. To make matters worse, Halley's tail suddenly ebbed at the beginning of April, leaving behind a small, condensed, nebulous mass with a stubby, fan-shaped appendage.

The leviathan turned out to be a mere tadpole!

A scientific gold mine

But while Halley disappointed the public, it proved to be an astronomical gold mine for astronomers. Within three weeks in March 1986, an international armada of spacecraft studied the comet: Japan launched Sakigake and Suisei; the Soviet Union sent VEGA 1 and VEGA 2; NASA contributed the International Cometary Explorer (ICE); and the European Space Agency, then a consortium of 11 countries, launched Giotto.

VEGA 1 and 2 and Giotto plunged deep into Halley's coma — the fuzzy, glowing cloud of gas and dust that surrounds the nucleus when it travels close to the sun — and revealed it to be an active, sputtering mass that responds violently to heating by the sun. Jets of dust were expelled from the nucleus with explosive intensity. And we discovered that the nucleus is encrusted in a dark shroud of its own debris and is as black as coal or velvet. Each VEGA spacecraft came to within about 5,300 miles (8,500 km) of Halley.

Giotto passed within just 375 miles (600 km) of the nucleus. More than 2,000 returned images showed that Halley's nucleus was larger than expected and shaped like a peanut or potato, measuring 9 miles (14 km) long and 5 miles (8 km) wide. The nucleus spins on its longest axis every 7.4 days, while the entire body appears to wobble in half that time. The images also revealed three "active regions," areas where volatile gases and dust escape when sunlight heats the surface. As the comet rotates, fresh ice enters the sunlight and sublimates; the escaping gas then drags entrained dust particles away from the nucleus.

Each VEGA spacecraft came to within about 5,300 miles (8,500 km) of Halley.

Giotto passed within just 375 miles (600 km) of the nucleus. More than 2,000 returned images showed that Halley's nucleus was larger than expected and shaped like a peanut or potato, measuring 9 miles (14 km) long and 5 miles (8 km) wide. The nucleus spins on its longest axis every 7.4 days, while the entire body appears to wobble in half that time. The images also revealed three "active regions," areas where volatile gases and dust escape when sunlight heats the surface. As the comet rotates, fresh ice enters the sunlight and sublimates; the escaping gas then drags entrained dust particles away from the nucleus.

So, from this tiny, jet-black, dust-encrusted nucleus came all the ingredients necessary to form the bright comet head and tail that branded it as a historically magnificent and awe-inspiring spectacle.

The spacecraft encounters transformed a disappointing naked-eye apparition into a landmark scientific campaign. Yet Halley's story did not end when the probes passed through its coma.

Surprises beyond 1986

Long after 1986, a receding Halley's Comet showed that it could still provide some surprises. On Feb. 12, 1991, between the orbits of Saturn and Uranus at 1.329 billion miles (2.138 billion km) from the sun, Halley was photographed from the European Southern Observatory in Chile by two Belgian astronomers. They had expected to find the comet appearing as nothing more than a faint speck of light. Instead, it appeared as a monstrous nebula 300 times brighter than expected; a massive outburst.

The cause of the dramatic flare-up remains a mystery. An unknown body may have collided with the comet. Another possibility is that the nucleus released a large amount of latent internal energy, although such a release would be unlikely so far from the sun. Highly energetic particles in the solar wind may also have reached the comet in sufficient numbers to heat its surface.

The road to 2061

On Dec. 8, 2023, Halley's Comet reached aphelion; the farthest point in its orbit from the sun.

Halley is expected to return in the summer of 2061, in circumstances that will largely mirror those of 1986 — but with one crucial difference. This time the comet will be fully visible on the same side of the sun as Earth and should appear at least 10 times brighter. In the morning sky, it will reach its northernmost position on July 24. It will then move rapidly southward as it enters the evening sky, gradually favoring more southerly locations. Even so, viewers at mid-northern latitudes should see an eye-catching object low in the west-northwest sky in early August.

And we don't have to wait until 2061 to experience Halley.

Like all comets, Halley's is a cosmic litterbug and, as such, it leaves behind in its wake a trail of — for lack of a better term — garbage, composed of tiny bits and crumbs of space debris that can produce beautiful incandescent trails upon impacting our atmosphere. Because they emanate from the constellation Orion, we call them the Orionid meteors, which will reach their peak on Oct. 21.

In a way, I guess you can call them "rock stars," but eventually, they fall down to Earth.

Joe Rao serves as an instructor and guest lecturer at New York's Hayden Planetarium. He writes about astronomy for Natural History magazine, Sky and Telescope, The Old Farmer's Almanac and other publications.

On Dec. 8, 2023, Halley's Comet reached aphelion; the farthest point in its orbit from the sun.

It will then move rapidly southward as it enters the evening sky, gradually favoring more southerly locations. Even so, viewers at mid-northern latitudes should see an eye-catching object low in the west-northwest sky in early August.

And we don't have to wait until 2061 to experience Halley.

Like all comets, Halley's is a cosmic litterbug and, as such, it leaves behind in its wake a trail of — for lack of a better term — garbage, composed of tiny bits and crumbs of space debris that can produce beautiful incandescent trails upon impacting our atmosphere. Because they emanate from the constellation Orion, we call them the Orionid meteors, which will reach their peak on Oct. 21.

In a way, I guess you can call them "rock stars," but eventually, they fall down to Earth.

]]> <![CDATA[ A faint glow from the early universe could help solve the mystery of dark energy ]]> Hydrogen may be the most common element in the cosmos, but scientists could use it to do something unique: uncover the nature of dark energy, the mysterious force driving the accelerating expansion of the universe.

This new line of dark energy investigation comes from the fact that researchers have determined that the CHIME (Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment) project can detect the faint radio glow of hydrogen from the universe's distant past.

Not only does this represent a faster and much less expensive way to investigate dark energy, but it is a major milestone for CHIME. The instrument was specifically devised to investigate dark energy and its pervasive influence.

"This is a completely new technique for probing the cosmos, delivered by an instrument that was conceived and built by Canadians," CHIME principal investigator Mark Halpern of the University of British Columbia said in a statement. "It's a bold new step in the global cosmology program and a Canadian success story."

Why is dark energy so problematic?

Dark energy is the mysterious force that is accelerating the expansion of the universe. It is so problematic for scientists because it started acting on the fabric of space only after the expansion triggered by the Big Bang had halted.

That's akin to pushing a child on a swing, watching it stop, and then seeing the swing start up again without a push. And, not only that, but the swing starts oscillating faster and faster. Consider scientists akin to very worried parents, who would really like to know where this ghostly push came from and how it is going to proceed.

Just as, if the push on the swing continues, the child could end up in the bushes, or in orbit, the strengthening of dark energy could result in the cold death of the cosmos, or even a "Big Rip" scenario that sees space shredded. Alternatively, if it weakens and allows gravity to reassert dominance, then the universe could collapse back in on itself, resulting in a "Big Crunch" ending that sees the cosmos compressed back into a singularity, as it was at the beginning of time.

Dark energy is now the dominant element of the universe, accounting for 68% of the universe's matter-energy budget. It's little wonder that scientists are very keen to know what this mysterious force is.

So how can hydrogen help the investigation of dark energy?

"Hydrogen is the most common element in the universe and the raw material from which stars form," team member Arnab Chakraborty of the University of Toronto said. "Its faint radio emission acts like a cosmic tracer, revealing how matter is distributed across space."

Previously, CHIME could map the distribution of hydrogen in the early universe but only by cross-correlating its observations with galaxy survey data from other telescopes, operations that cost millions of dollars and can only focus on regions of the universe dense enough to form stars. CHIME has now shown it can map the radio glow of hydrogen all on its own.

Indeed, the team has already begun making steps in this direction using just a tiny fraction of existing CHIME data. Using 94 nights of observations from 2019, they detected a hydrogen signal from when the universe was just 5 billion years old.

"Our data indicate that roughly 2% of the hydrogen in the universe was in neutral atomic form at this time, broadly consistent with other measurements," team member Shabbir Shaikh of Arizona State University said. "By measuring how that hydrogen is distributed and clustered, CHIME gives us a new way to test our understanding of how galaxies form and evolve."

CHIME has now collected seven years of data, and using this, the team is hoping to probe the distribution of hydrogen back to 3 billion years after the Big Bang.

The team's research was published across two papers in The Astrophysical Journal.

]]> <![CDATA[ SpaceX launches Falcon 9 Starlink mission for 1st time in more than 3 weeks (photos) ]]> SpaceX just broke an uncharacteristically long Starlink launch drought.

The company sent 27 of its Starlink internet satellites to low Earth orbit (LEO) today (Oct. 12), launching them atop a Falcon 9 rocket from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base at 8:28 p.m. EDT (5:28 p.m. local time; 0028 GMT on Oct. 13)

It was the first Starlink mission for a Falcon 9 since Sept. 19, which was another 27-satellite liftoff from Vandenberg. For some perspective on this recent gap: Between Aug. 19 and Sept. 6, a span of 19 days, SpaceX launched seven Starlink missions with Falcon 9s.

SpaceX did loft a batch of Starlinks after that, but it wasn't aboard a Falcon 9. The company's Starship megarocket carried 26 next-gen Starlink V3 craft on its 14th test flight, which took place on Sept. 28.

Starship reached orbit for the first time ever on Flight 14, and it deployed the Starlinks successfully as well. This will happen many more times going forward, if all goes to plan: The Starlink V3 constellation will eventually consist of about 100,000 satellites, all of which will fly on Starship, Elon Musk has said.

Indeed, SpaceX plans to sunset the Falcon 9 and its cousin, the Falcon Heavy, in the next few years, shifting their duties over to the fully reusable, far more powerful Starship, which remains in the test-flight phase.

That shift will be a big one for the spaceflight community, for the Falcon 9 is the workhorse rocket of its generation. In 2025, for example, it flew 165 times — roughly the same number as the rest of the world's orbital launchers combined. Nearly three-quarters of those Falcon 9 launches were Starlink missions.

Things have slowed down a bit in 2026. Today's flight was the 112th Falcon 9 liftoff of the year, and the 82nd in service of the Starlink megaconstellation, which currently consists of more than 11,100 active satellites.

Previous Booster 1088 launches

NROL-126 | Transporter-12 | SPHEREx | NROL-57 | USSF-366 | 14 Starlink missions

All went according to plan on today's launch. The Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth as planned, touching down about 8.5 minutes after launch on the drone ship "Of Course I Still Love You," which was stationed in the Pacific Ocean. It was the 20th launch and landing for this particular booster, which is designated B1088.

The rocket's expendable upper stage, meanwhile, delivered the 27 spacecraft to LEO, deploying them there 62 minutes after liftoff, SpaceX announced via X.

]]> <![CDATA[ SpaceX successfully launches 6,300 pounds of cargo to the International Space Station ]]>

SpaceX launched its latest cargo mission to the International Space Station (ISS) on Tuesday morning (Oct. 13).

A Falcon 9 rocket launched a robotic Dragon capsule to the orbiting lab from Florida's Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Tuesday at 6:35 a.m. EDT (1035 GMT).

The launch kicks off the CRS-35 mission, so named because it will be the 35th that SpaceX flies under a Commercial Resupply Services contract with NASA.

If all goes according to plan, Dragon will reach the International Space Station (ISS) on Thursday (Oct. 15), docking autonomously to the space-facing port of its Harmony module at around 11 a.m. EDT (1500 GMT). You can watch the arrival here at Space.com as well; coverage will start at 9:15 a.m. EDT (1315 GMT).

CRS-35 will deliver 6,300 pounds (2,860 kilograms) of supplies to the astronauts aboard the orbiting lab, including the final set of International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Arrays (iROSAs), which will boost the orbiting lab's energy budget.

There's also quite a bit of scientific gear heading up on the flight.

Dragon "will deliver hardware to manufacture artificial retinas in microgravity to help restore vision on Earth and 3D heart tissue models to advance large‑scale drug testing on future missions," NASA officials wrote in a CRS-35 launch preview on Oct. 7.

"The spacecraft will carry materials to study how a new type of glass forms in microgravity and brain organoids that could reveal treatment targets for neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and multiple sclerosis," they added.

Dragon will stay attached to the ISS for about a month, then head back down to Earth with scientific experiments and other hardware. It will splash down safely under parachutes in the Pacific Ocean off the California coast.

SpaceX's Dragon is the only currently operational freighter that can carry cargo in the downward direction. The other three — Russia's Progress, Japan's HTV-X and Northrop Grumman's Cygnus XL — are all expendable, burning up in Earth's atmosphere after their time at the ISS is done.

Editor's note: This story was updated at 6:59 a.m. EDT on Oct. 13 with news of a successful launch.

]]> <![CDATA[ Astronomers witness supermassive black hole gorge on a cosmic meal before 'burping' radio jets 300 days later ]]> Using the NASA X-ray spacecraft Swift combined with radio observations, astronomers have observed a supermassive black hole burping radio jets 300 days after a heavy cosmic meal. The team was also able to roughly estimate the mass of this feeding cosmic titan, which sits at the heart of the Perseus Cluster, a massive collection of thousands of galaxies.

The black hole sits at the center of the galaxy NGC 1275, located around 225 light-years away, and is the brightest galaxy of the Perseus Cluster. The supermassive black hole first flared in X-rays, which indicated an increase in the rate at which it was accreting matter. Actively feeding supermassive black holes sit in regions called active galactic nuclei (AGNs), with their immense gravity heating surrounding matter, causing them to glow brightly. These emissions are boosted by material channeled to the poles of the central black hole, from where it is blasted out as powerful twin jets that shine across the electromagnetic spectrum, particularly in radio waves.

The observation of the following radio jet from the AGN at the heart of NGC 1275 via flaring in radio waves is crucial for understanding the relationship between the disk of matter that surrounds and feeds the black hole, called an accretion disk, and the jets it launches. This so-called disk-jet coupling is key to developing a better picture of how black holes influence star formation in the galaxies in which they sit, and thus the growth of those galaxies.

Making these observations is no mean feat. The ideal spacecraft for observing X-ray emissions is Chandra, but it doesn't observe NGC 1275 frequently enough to observe its long-term behaviour. NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory may lack the power of Chandra, but having launched in 2004, it has collected a vast amount of data regarding NGC 1275 and its central supermassive black hole.

"It is fairly difficult to see the inner region of this AGN because NGC 1275 is at the center of the massive Perseus cluster of galaxies, which adds additional light to our observations," team leader Sarah Ketchum of the University of Michigan told Space.com. "We developed a model that allowed us to remove the cluster emission from archival Swift data, and in doing so, we were able to see the changes in the X-ray flux from gas accreting onto the black hole in NGC 1275, from 2007 to 2025."

Ketchum added that the capabilities of Swift were key to this investigation of NGC 1275, which is the ideal laboratory for the study of disk-jet coupling.

"There have been studies on other galaxies with AGN that show evidence of coupling between gas accretion traced in X-ray light and gas ejection in jets, traced in radio light. But NGC 1275 reveals the impact of black hole jets on large spatial scales better than any other system," the University of Michigan researcher continued.

This black hole didn't eat a star

Ketchum and colleagues saw the strongest ever X-ray flare from NGC 1275 in Feb. 2023. Lasting less than 60 days and consisting of two 5-day blasts, this episode saw a doubling of the X-ray brightness of the AGN at the heart of NGC 1275.

The flaring was so extreme that the team had to rule out a tidal disruption event (TDE) as the cause. These occur when an unfortunate star's orbit brings it too close to the immense gravitational influence of a supermassive black hole. This influence generates intense tidal forces that simultaneously squash and squeeze the star, "speghettifying" it and allowing the black hole to snack on some plasma pasta.

"We were able to rule out TDEs as a cause," Ketchum said. "Thus, the flaring was likely caused by a spike in the rate at which matter accreted onto the black hole."

Using Swift data, the team was able to infer the radius over which the AGN emits radiation. Because the size of a black hole is directly correlated with its mass, this meant that the researchers were able to constrain the mass of the black hole at the heart of NGC 1275. They determined that this supermassive black hole has a mass somewhere between 100 million times the mass of the sun and 1 billion solar masses.

The team then compared their data to known radio data to better understand the relationship between the X-ray emission and the radio jets that disrupt gas in NGC 1275.

Ketchum added that she and her colleagues found tentative evidence of around a 300-day delay between the X-ray flaring and the radio wave emission. This indicates the time it takes plasma to travel from the base of the jet to a knot or shock created when it hits surrounding gas or dust.

"This should be tested further in the future. Our X-ray data only sparsely sample the changes in NGC 1275," Ketchum said. "This makes it difficult to determine an exact relationship between the X-ray and radio radiation for large portions of our light curve, so we would need more X-ray data to further study this connection."

The researcher added that if the X-ray flares are produced close to the black hole, an echo of these flares should be seen coming from the accretion disk.

"An emission line from neutral iron is seen in data from NGC 1275, and this may be the echo. However, we likely need many observations with XMM-Newton and XRISM ( X-Ray Imaging and Spectroscopy Mission) to really establish that connection," Ketchum concluded.

The team's research has been accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal Letters, with a pre-peer-review version available on the repository site arXiv.

]]> <![CDATA[ The moon could turn astronauts into 'walking, high voltage capacitors' that accidentally zap spacecraft ]]> NASA is asking for ideas to stop static electricity from zapping astronauts or critical hardware during moon missions.

The agency opened a "Lunar Grounding Challenge" to avoid situations where an astronaut on the moon could become "a walking, high voltage capacitor." Submissions for the $150,000 competition are due Jan. 15 and you can see the requirements here.

NASA is hoping to put astronaut boots at the lunar south pole in 2028 during the Artemis 4 or 5 missions, on the first landing mission since NASA's Apollo 17 in 1972. But simulations suggest that both "tribocharging" (electric-charge transfer between two objects) and plasma charging (from ambient gas in the region) could build up electric charge on spacesuits. "This problem is severely compounded when entering lunar shadows and permanently shadowed regions," the agency wrote, referring to deeply cratered areas where the sun does not touch the lunar surface.

The concern is that astronauts' spacesuits could become electrically charged, as there would be an excess of electrons (negatively charged particles) compared with ions (positively charged) in these areas.

]]> <![CDATA[ The 'Halloween Fireballs' are coming. Here's what to expect from the Taurids this October ]]> They don't produce anything like the torrent of "shooting stars" associated with August's Perseids or December's Geminids, but the Taurid meteor showers have something else going for them — fireballs.

The Taurids are famous for occasionally producing exceptionally bright, slow-moving meteors that can streak dramatically across the night sky from September to December. As a bonus, they're visible from both the Northern and Southern hemispheres. That's because they appear to emanate from the constellation Taurus, which sits close to the ecliptic, the apparent path the sun takes across the sky as Earth orbits around it.

The Taurids are actually two closely related showers — the Southern Taurids and Northern Taurids — whose activity overlaps in late October and November. That's why they're known informally by skywatchers as the "Halloween fireballs." The broad overlapping peaks make the Taurids less about watching on one particular night and more about keeping an eye on the night sky for several weeks. Both have their radiant points — the place in the night sky where their "shooting stars" appear to come from — close to the famous Pleiades (M45) open cluster of stars in the constellation Taurus.

There's another tempting reason to watch the Taurids in 2026 — moonlight will cause little interference around the main peaks.

When are the Southern Taurids?

The Southern Taurids are already underway. According to the American Meteor Society, they're active from Sept. 20 through Nov. 20, with two distinct components. The annual component peaks around Oct. 14, while a component particularly associated with fireballs peaks overnight on Nov. 4-5. That's the night to circle if you're hoping to see one of the "Halloween Fireballs."

However, don't expect a conventional meteor storm. The Southern Taurids have an average zenithal hourly rate of about five meteors per hour. ZHR describes how many meteors an observer could theoretically see under ideal conditions with the shower's radiant directly overhead. In practice, observers see fewer, so this is not a chance to gather friends for a special show, as with the Perseids.

What the Southern Taurids lack in quantity, however, they can make up for in quality. Their meteors strike Earth's atmosphere at about 17 miles (27 kilometers) per second. That's relatively slow for a meteor, helping make some Taurids conspicuous as they travel across the sky. You don't see a Taurid meteor; you watch it.

If clouds allow, conditions should be favorable around Nov. 4-5. The moon will be absent most of the night, rising a couple of hours before dawn as a 17%-illuminated waning crescent — too dim to affect visibility of meteors.

When are the Northern Taurids?

The Northern Taurids begin later, becoming active on Oct. 20 and continuing through Dec. 10, according to the American Meteor Society. They're expected to peak overnight on Nov. 11-12.

Once again, rates are low — around five meteors per hour under ideal conditions — but fireballs are possible. Northern Taurid meteors enter the atmosphere at around 18 miles (29 km) per second, similarly as slow as their southern counterparts.

Observing conditions at the peak should be excellent. The moon will be a slender 5%-illuminated waxing crescent and will be practically absent from the night sky overnight on Nov. 11-12, leaving the night dark.

The distinction between the two Taurid showers isn't particularly important if you're simply outside hoping to see a fireball. In late October and early November, both streams are active at the same time, potentially producing around 10 Taurids per hour under clear, moon-free conditions.

Why are Taurids called the 'Halloween Fireballs'?

The nickname comes partly from timing. Their maxima are also broad rather than sharp. According to EarthSky, the Taurids tend to "ramble along" over the period, becoming particularly noticeable when the two branches overlap from late October into early November — Halloween.

It's also a reference to their tendency to produce fireballs, exceptionally bright meteors caused when larger pieces of space debris plunge into Earth's atmosphere.

Some years are considerably better for Taurid fireballs than others, and it's impossible to tell for sure in advance. EarthSky notes that enhanced displays occurred in 2008, 2015 and 2022, when Earth encountered concentrations of larger debris within the stream. However, don't expect a repeat in 2026 — the next predicted Taurid fireball swarm isn't expected until 2032.

That doesn't mean there won't be fireballs this year, only that an unusually high number isn't predicted.

What causes the Taurid meteor showers?

Both Taurid meteor showers are linked to Comet 2P/Encke, a three-mile-wide (4.8-kilometer) comet that circles the sun every 3.25 years — the shortest known cometary orbit, according to NASA. However, the Taurids belong to a much larger complex of dust, rocks, comets and asteroids, possibly created when a much bigger object fragmented thousands of years ago. Each fall, Earth crosses different parts of this sprawling debris stream, producing the overlapping Northern and Southern Taurids and, occasionally, the larger fragments that create spectacular fireballs.

How to see the Taurid meteor showers

Both showers appear to originate from Taurus, a constellation that rises during the evening and climbs higher into the sky as the night progresses. Around midnight, Taurus is well placed for many observers.

However, there's no need to find Taurus. Meteors can appear anywhere in the sky, and staring directly at the radiant can actually mean seeing shorter meteor trails. The best advice is to treat the period as a great time for naked-eye stargazing, with the usual rules applying — find somewhere away from bright lights with as wide a view of the sky as possible, and give your eyes about 20 minutes to adjust to the darkness. Binoculars and telescopes will restrict your field of view and make meteor watching impossible.

Above all, be patient. The Taurids are a slow burn in every sense — low rates, slow-moving meteors and weeks of activity. But if one of those meteors happens to be a brilliant fireball, it could easily be one of the most memorable "shooting stars" you see all year.

]]> <![CDATA[ On this day in space! Oct. 12, 1964: The Soviet Union launches Voskhod 1, the 1st multi-person cosmonaut crew, into space ]]>

On Oct. 12, 1964, the Soviet Union launched Voskhod 1, a 24-hour crewed mission that achieved several "firsts" for human spaceflight. This was the first time that a spacecraft carried more than one person into orbit, with three cosmonauts packed inside the spacecraft.

Only two cosmonauts were originally supposed to fly on this mission, but Soviet politicians pressured the Russian space program to add one more. This left no room for spacesuits on board, so this also became the first spaceflight without spacesuits.

Two of the crewmembers, an engineer and a doctor, became the first civilians to go to space.

Why it mattered

Voskhod 1 served as yet another first for the Soviet Union during a space race kicked off by the launch of Sputnik 1 in 1957 and followed up by the first human spaceflight with Yuri Gagarin in 1961. And while the United States did follow up with its one human spaceflights, until Oct. 12, 1964, every mission had one person on board.

That changed with Voskhod 1, which crammed three man into a spacecraft not much larger than the Soviet Union's one-person Vostok spacecraft. At the time, NASA was develoing the two-person Gemini spacecraft, which prompted the Soviet Union's then leader to push for an edge.

"Soviet leader [Nikita] Khrushchev contacted Korolev and ordered him to convert the Vostok spacecraft into a vehicle capable of carrying not two, but three cosmonauts," according to space historian Asif Siddiqi, referring to Sergei Korolev, chief designer of the Soviet space program.

In order to fit a three people inside, the Voskhod 1 cosmonauts - commander Vladimir Komarov and his crew Konstantin Feoktistov and Boris Yegorov - did not wear spacesuits traditionally used for launch and landing, adding substantial risk to the flight. They also stayed inside their spacecraft when it landed, unlike Vostok crews like Gagarin, who parachuted out of them after reentry.

The Voskhod 1 mission lasted just over 24 hours, during which its crew performed experimented with the behavior of liquids and gases in microgravity and photographed the Earth.

NASA's first multi-crew mission, Gemini 3, would launch about six month later on March 23, 1965.

]]> <![CDATA[ Namibian salt flats look like an alien planet | Space photo of the day for Oct. 12, 2026 ]]>

A neon blue pool swirls amongst what look like clouds, all surrounded by a bright red stretch of land. This might look like the surface of an alien planet, but it's actually a salt flat right here on Earth, seen from space.

What is it?

Etosha National Park in northern Namibia hosts the largest salt pan, or piece of land covered with salt and other minerals, in the country.

This image of the Etosha Pan was captured on April 5 of this year by Europe's Copernicus Sentinel-2 mission, which consists of two identical satellites in the same orbit.

The Sentinel-2 pair observe and capture imagery of our planet in different wavelengths using a high-resolution multispectral imager that can see 13 different spectral bands, or ranges of wavelengths.

By looking at our planet from space, and observing it through different wavelengths and colors, we can better understand Earth's topography and how it changes over time. With this image, researchers can better understand this landmark in Namibia, a nation in southwestern Africa.

Why is it incredible?

While this image is strikingly beautiful, the Etosha Pan doesn't exactly look like this in real life. If you were standing close to the pan in the national park, it would look bright white.

While this is a real image, false color has been added, which allows scientists to separate different types of vegetation and topography.

With the false color, the vegetation surrounding the salt pan appears in shades of red, while the salt pan itself looks like a mix of bright, light and dark blues with cloudy sediment floating around.

The varied vegetation captured in this false-color image includes grassland, savannas and mopane trees, which appear bright red. These trees are not only a dominant type of vegetation in areas of this park, they also provide essential shelter and habitats for local wildlife, including elephants, giraffe and leopards.

]]> <![CDATA[ How the impossible geometry of 'Tomb Raider III''s UFO level was made ]]> "Tomb Raider" celebrates its 30th anniversary this month. While many remember the iconic T-Rex or locking Winston the Butler in the freezer, many forget about the UFO in 1998’s "Tomb Raider III"; a mysterious alien craft that worked a lot like Doctor Who’s TARDIS.

Coming off the back of the hugely successful "Tomb Raider 2", developer Core Design had big plans for the third entry, including kayaking, those iconic London levels, and, of course, a level featuring a UFO in Area 51. Although it looked small on the outside, the UFO featured multiple floors for players to explore as they searched for a vital artifact, all as enemies swarmed in.

Now, I'm something of a Tomb Raider historian, and my upcoming book — "The Making of Tomb Raider: 1997-2000" (available from October 30) — goes into detail about the making of "Tomb Raider III", "Tomb Raider IV", and other games in the series during those three years. While writing the book, I spoke to level designer Richard Morton about how the physics-defying UFO was made and how shows like "The X-Files" inspired him and the team.

The Lone Gunwoman

When you start "Tomb Raider III", you find Lara in India, stumbling across one of four artifacts. After completing India, you can choose between London, South Pacific, and Nevada to collect the other artifacts before reaching the final section in Antarctica.

Richard Morton was one of the designers for "Tomb Raider III", who took on South Pacific and some of Nevada, a location that Neal Boyd had already begun work on before he moved to "Project Eden". Eventually, Lara would find herself in Area 51, with the final part of the level taking place in a UFO that houses the artifact she seeks.

“Area 51 was a bit of a team effort,” reveals Morton. “The part where the rocket launches, Neal did a lot of that stuff. So much of that level is his work, as well as some of the other routes. Andy Sandham helped in finishing off that level, too. And then the bit with the UFO, that was mine.”

Of course, a level called Area 51 needed aliens. In the late 1990s, UFOs were everywhere, ranging from TV shows like The X-Files to countless documentaries on whether aliens were real.

“We knew Area 51 had to have aliens in it in some form. And we did put some down on operating tables – we were all influenced by films and shows like 'The X-Files' and 'Independence Day', which were around at the time of TR3.”

You’d run past the UFO at certain points in between toggling switches, collecting keys, and even launching a rocket. Eventually, you’d unlock a door, letting you in to reveal an impossibly large interior. But all wasn’t as it seemed, and the journey to get here was fraught with challenges.

“I was working quite late one evening, and it wasn't a UFO to start with. I was working on the level and suddenly wondered what would happen if I had three rooms next to each other, with the room in the middle that was only the width of the portal,” explains Morton. “Then I’d link that to a separate room that was only visible inside the portal. I then somehow managed to build this impossible room that was surrounded by eight rooms – the only way I could get it to work. And it did, but it worked horizontally – it was just like Valve's 'Portal', but nine years before.”

AI programmer Tom Scutt, who had joined the team to improve the artificial intelligence for the enemies, worked with Morton to see how a portal could work in the level.

“Tom loved it, but I think he started doing some tests around it – this was just a portal in a room to see if it could be used. Soon after, he explained to me that enemies wouldn't work with it without being heavily reworked, because of how the navigation worked with the enemies,” Morton explains. “So if Lara went through a portal to 'another world', for example, the enemies wouldn't know; they'd just stay in the same room. So all in all, they basically said that they loved it, but you can't do it - and yet I kept trying.”

The truth is in there

With Area 51 taking shape and the portal idea becoming viable, Morton realized that the two could become one, resulting in the UFO. “The next night, I decided to build a UFO, which we'd already built within the level in this rough shape in one of the hangars at the end of the level.”

That night, Morton cracked it, meaning the inside of the UFO could now be far bigger. “I built a ladder going up from the entrance, which went straight up through the tiny UFO model, which was only three by three blocks, with a one-block hole going up into it. So I remade the same trick from the night before, only vertically, and it worked!”

Still, despite getting the trick to work, more had to be done to ensure no bugs would emerge during this final section of the level.

“Once you got inside the UFO, I think we had to do a tiny bit of fiddling around, just to make the enemies warp inside the UFO. But they'd only try to attack you when you were in the UFO. I think we triggered them once you got in there and de-triggered them once you came out, just to stop them from firing at you when you weren't in there, just to keep that illusion of this TARDIS UFO going.”

Programmer Martin Gibbins, who had previously warned that the UFO would break everything, was won over by it. “Despite the UFO being Richard's idea, that was a testament to Gavin Rummery's ridiculous portal system. It had a single-block doorway into what was effectively a room. That was the clip window for the rest of the world, so you could do whatever you'd like inside of it. He got it working, and I thought it was great.”

For its time, it was an amazing feat on PlayStation and PC. With this being the third mainline "Tomb Raider" game, some players felt that the series was getting stale. But it was moments like the UFO and discovering it was far bigger than many initially thought that stuck with players, and still does to this day.

Unfortunately, another moment like the UFO would not happen in subsequent games, with the pressure of making the Thanksgiving deadline looming over the team. But Morton reveals that the team did speak about what could have alternatively happened at the end of the level.

"I think we talked about having a portal room that took you to another area that could have been either another location on Earth or another location across the galaxy. But obviously, we just didn't have time to do anything like that. It would have been awesome, though.”

However, after Morton spent two evenings trying to get the UFO to work and some on the team worried that it would break the game, it became a big highlight of "Tomb Raider III".

“When I showed the team the UFO, they were basically trembling, thinking, 'What have you done now!?' And we found out that it did work, and they ended up loving it. Looking back, I couldn't believe that I'd pulled it off, to be honest. I couldn't believe that the engine didn't just crash the game every time the camera looked into that portal. It didn't crash, and I thought, ‘Wow, that's awesome,’ at the time.”

The impossible geometry of the "Tomb Raider III" UFO is indeed an impressive spectacle, even almost 30 years later. ]]> https://www.space.com/entertainment/space-games/how-the-impossible-geometry-of-tomb-raider-iiis-ufo-level-was-made TAF37XKkXJe6KwXgLjHwvQ Mon, 12 Oct 2026 14:00:00 +0000 Mon, 12 Oct 2026 14:28:50 +0000 false false false

"Tomb Raider" celebrates its 30th anniversary this month. While many remember the iconic T-Rex or locking Winston the Butler in the freezer, many forget about the UFO in 1998’s "Tomb Raider III"; a mysterious alien craft that worked a lot like Doctor Who’s TARDIS.

Coming off the back of the hugely successful "Tomb Raider 2", developer Core Design had big plans for the third entry, including kayaking, those iconic London levels, and, of course, a level featuring a UFO in Area 51. Although it looked small on the outside, the UFO featured multiple floors for players to explore as they searched for a vital artifact, all as enemies swarmed in.

Now, I'm something of a Tomb Raider historian, and my upcoming book — "The Making of Tomb Raider: 1997-2000" (available from October 30) — goes into detail about the making of "Tomb Raider III", "Tomb Raider IV", and other games in the series during those three years. While writing the book, I spoke to level designer Richard Morton about how the physics-defying UFO was made and how shows like "The X-Files" inspired him and the team.

The Lone Gunwoman

When you start "Tomb Raider III", you find Lara in India, stumbling across one of four artifacts. After completing India, you can choose between London, South Pacific, and Nevada to collect the other artifacts before reaching the final section in Antarctica.

Richard Morton was one of the designers for "Tomb Raider III", who took on South Pacific and some of Nevada, a location that Neal Boyd had already begun work on before he moved to "Project Eden". Eventually, Lara would find herself in Area 51, with the final part of the level taking place in a UFO that houses the artifact she seeks.

“Area 51 was a bit of a team effort,” reveals Morton. “The part where the rocket launches, Neal did a lot of that stuff. So much of that level is his work, as well as some of the other routes. Andy Sandham helped in finishing off that level, too. And then the bit with the UFO, that was mine.”

Of course, a level called Area 51 needed aliens. In the late 1990s, UFOs were everywhere, ranging from TV shows like The X-Files to countless documentaries on whether aliens were real.

“We knew Area 51 had to have aliens in it in some form. And we did put some down on operating tables – we were all influenced by films and shows like 'The X-Files' and 'Independence Day', which were around at the time of TR3.”

You’d run past the UFO at certain points in between toggling switches, collecting keys, and even launching a rocket. Eventually, you’d unlock a door, letting you in to reveal an impossibly large interior. But all wasn’t as it seemed, and the journey to get here was fraught with challenges.

“I was working quite late one evening, and it wasn't a UFO to start with. I was working on the level and suddenly wondered what would happen if I had three rooms next to each other, with the room in the middle that was only the width of the portal,” explains Morton. “Then I’d link that to a separate room that was only visible inside the portal. I then somehow managed to build this impossible room that was surrounded by eight rooms – the only way I could get it to work. And it did, but it worked horizontally – it was just like Valve's 'Portal', but nine years before.”

AI programmer Tom Scutt, who had joined the team to improve the artificial intelligence for the enemies, worked with Morton to see how a portal could work in the level.

“Tom loved it, but I think he started doing some tests around it – this was just a portal in a room to see if it could be used. Soon after, he explained to me that enemies wouldn't work with it without being heavily reworked, because of how the navigation worked with the enemies,” Morton explains. “So if Lara went through a portal to 'another world', for example, the enemies wouldn't know; they'd just stay in the same room. So all in all, they basically said that they loved it, but you can't do it - and yet I kept trying.”

The truth is in there

With Area 51 taking shape and the portal idea becoming viable, Morton realized that the two could become one, resulting in the UFO. “The next night, I decided to build a UFO, which we'd already built within the level in this rough shape in one of the hangars at the end of the level.”

That night, Morton cracked it, meaning the inside of the UFO could now be far bigger. “I built a ladder going up from the entrance, which went straight up through the tiny UFO model, which was only three by three blocks, with a one-block hole going up into it. So I remade the same trick from the night before, only vertically, and it worked!”

Still, despite getting the trick to work, more had to be done to ensure no bugs would emerge during this final section of the level.

“Once you got inside the UFO, I think we had to do a tiny bit of fiddling around, just to make the enemies warp inside the UFO. But they'd only try to attack you when you were in the UFO. I think we triggered them once you got in there and de-triggered them once you came out, just to stop them from firing at you when you weren't in there, just to keep that illusion of this TARDIS UFO going.”

Programmer Martin Gibbins, who had previously warned that the UFO would break everything, was won over by it. “Despite the UFO being Richard's idea, that was a testament to Gavin Rummery's ridiculous portal system. It had a single-block doorway into what was effectively a room. That was the clip window for the rest of the world, so you could do whatever you'd like inside of it. He got it working, and I thought it was great.”

For its time, it was an amazing feat on PlayStation and PC. With this being the third mainline "Tomb Raider" game, some players felt that the series was getting stale. But it was moments like the UFO and discovering it was far bigger than many initially thought that stuck with players, and still does to this day.

Unfortunately, another moment like the UFO would not happen in subsequent games, with the pressure of making the Thanksgiving deadline looming over the team. But Morton reveals that the team did speak about what could have alternatively happened at the end of the level.

"I think we talked about having a portal room that took you to another area that could have been either another location on Earth or another location across the galaxy. But obviously, we just didn't have time to do anything like that. It would have been awesome, though.”

However, after Morton spent two evenings trying to get the UFO to work and some on the team worried that it would break the game, it became a big highlight of "Tomb Raider III".

“When I showed the team the UFO, they were basically trembling, thinking, 'What have you done now!?' And we found out that it did work, and they ended up loving it. Looking back, I couldn't believe that I'd pulled it off, to be honest. I couldn't believe that the engine didn't just crash the game every time the camera looked into that portal. It didn't crash, and I thought, ‘Wow, that's awesome,’ at the time.”

The impossible geometry of the "Tomb Raider III" UFO is indeed an impressive spectacle, even almost 30 years later. If you’re interested in seeing how the TARDIS/UFO works, you can play "Tomb Raider III" via the Remastered collection, available on PlayStation 4/5, Xbox Series, Nintendo Switch 1/2, iOS, Android, and PC via Steam.

If you want to know more about "Tomb Raider 3" and its enigmatic UFO, "The Making of Tomb Raider: 1997-2000" is available from October 30 via Pen and Sword, Amazon, and other retailers.

   <title>Tejc změní rozvodovou novelu. Dítě má více chránit před násilným rodičem</title>

   <description>Vláda 12. října schválila návrh ministerstva spravedlnosti, který upravuje sporné části rozvodové novely schválené minulou vládou a platné od 1. ledna 2026. Změny reagují na výhrady odborníků i zkušenosti soudů a mají lépe chránit děti, zejména v případech domácího násilí, vyhrocených sporů mezi rodiči nebo jiných situací, kdy může být ohrožena bezpečnost dětí. Novela zároveň přináší jasnější pravidla pro rozhodování soudů a klade větší důraz na nejlepší zájem dítěte.</description>

   <description>Na základě vládního nařízení se od Nového roku mění výše záloh pojistného na sociální a zdravotní pojištění pro živnostníky.   <item>
   <title>Češi to nevědí. Z lesa lze brát jen větve určitých rozměrů, jinak hrozí pokuty</title>
   <link>https://www.denik.cz/ekonomika/cesko-pozor-na-noseni-drive-a-chrasti-z-lesa-hrozi-vysoke-pokuty/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed-vse&utm_campaign=ceskolipsky.denik.cz&utm_content=ekonomika</link>
   <description>Podzimní chlad a také rostoucí ceny energií lákají lidi do lesa pro palivo zdarma. Přitom co smí návštěvník odnést, je přesně vymezeno a za porušení pravidel hrozí desetitisícové pokuty, v případě trestného činu i vězení. Lesníci i ochránci přírody navíc varují, že nadměrný odběr dříví z lesa lesnímu prostředí nesvědčí.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Nelegálně přejít hranici do Česka bude trestné, dohodla se koalice, říká Okamura</title>
      <link>https://www.idnes.cz/zpravy/domaci/nelegalne-prijit-do-ceska-ma-byt-znovu-trestne-dohodla-s-koalice-tvrdi-okamura.A261013_122925_domaci_kop#utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=zpravodaj&utm_content=main</link>
      <description>Nelegální překročení české státní hranice má být znovu trestným činem. Na přípravě takového návrhu se podle Tomia Okamury na návrh SPD domluvila vládní koalice. Má se týkat jen občanů třetích zemí, kteří se do Česka pokusí nelegálně dostat. </description>

    <item>
      <title>Trump rekordně vydělává. Na úřadu se obohacuje, míní většina Američanů</title>
      <link>https://www.idnes.cz/zpravy/zahranicni/trump-rekordne-vydelava-na-uradu-se-obohacuje-mini-vetsina-americanu.A261013_140136_zahranicni_bro#utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=zpravodaj&utm_content=main</link>
      <description>Většina Američanů se domnívá, že americký prezident Donald Trump z úřadu neeticky či dokonce nezákonně profituje a že ho víc než pomoc obyčejným lidem zajímá vlastní bohatství. Vyplývá to z průzkumu agentury AP a společnosti NORC. Trumpův rodinný byznys mezitím i vzhledem k jeho politice hlásí rekordní příjmy z nových podniků.</description>
      <pubDate>Tue, 13 Oct 2026 12:08:00 GMT</pubDate>

    <item>

      <description>Socha Františka Palackého na stejnojmenném náměstí v Praze prochází generální očistou. Firma Kärcher se pustila odstraňování viditelných nečistot, které se na této pražské památce za poslední roky nakumulovaly. Hotovo by mohlo být nejpozději do středy.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Maďarsko chce do eurozóny. Vláda chystá nové daně a omezení státních výdajů</title>
      <link>https://www.idnes.cz/ekonomika/zahranicni/madarsko-vlada-euro-prijeti-meny-reformy-magyar-orban-zmena.A261013_120958_eko-zahranicni_jla#utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=zpravodaj&utm_content=main</link>
      <description>Po šestnácti letech vlády Viktora Orbána se Maďarsko připravuje na další významnou změnu. Od května nový premiér Péter Magyar chce zemi přivést do eurozóny a postupně nahradit forint společnou evropskou měnou. Jeho plán však naráží na špatný stav veřejných financí. </description>

<description>České Radiokomunikace (CRA) od leto&#353;ního listopadu reorganizují svůj stále rostoucí a důležitěj&#353;í byznys s datovými centry, cloudem a provozem serverů. Z CRA budou prvního listopadu vyčleněna aktiva do dvou nástupnických firem, kterými budou Datové centrum Lužice a Cloud4com. CRA jsou v obou jediným akcionářem.</description>

<item>
<title>Krabicovým hrám odzvonilo. Legendární český e-shop otočil kormidlo a hlásí rekordní čísla</title>
<link>https://www.lupa.cz/aktuality/krabicovym-hram-odzvonilo-legendarni-cesky-e-shop-otocil-kormidlo-a-hlasi-rekordni-cisla/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=text&utm_campaign=rss</link>
<description>Českému internetovému obchodu Xzone se podařil velký obrat. Firma před lety vznikla jako e-shop specializovaný na hry, konzole a příslu&#353;enství kolem. Prodeje krabicových verzí her ov&#353;em s nástupem digitální distribuce typu Steam nebo PlayStation Network ustoupily do pozadí. Xzone zareagovalo příklonem k merchandisingu, oblečení, deskovkám a dal&#353;ímu popkulturnímu sortimentu, což zafungovalo.</description>

</item>
<item>
<title>Třetina dospělých už řešila s AI svou psychickou krizi, stát nyní chce řešit, jak téma pojmout</title>
<link>https://www.lupa.cz/aktuality/tretina-dospelych-uz-resila-s-ai-svou-psychickou-krizi-stat-nyni-chce-resit-jak-tema-pojmout/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=text&utm_campaign=rss</link>
<description>Lidé se stále častěji obracejí na umělou inteligenci i s problémy, které se týkají jejich psychiky. Podle jarního výzkumu ji v souvislosti s du&#353;evním zdravím během předchozích 30 dnů použila víc než polovina lidí ve věku 18 až 34 let. Téměř třetina uživatelů s ní už ře&#353;ila psychickou krizi nebo akutní stres. A podobný podíl ji alespoň někdy využil místo odborné pomoci. Ministerstvo zdravotnictví proto při&#353;lo s oznámením, že chystá doporučení, jak AI při ře&#353;ení psychických potíží bezpečně používat. Téma začlenilo i do národního akčního plánu.</description>

<author>redakce@lupa.cz (Lupa.cz: Iva Brejlová)</author>
<pubDate>Tue, 13 Oct 2026 11:20:52 GMT</pubDate>

<guid isPermaLink="false">www.lupa.cz-actuality-18548</guid>


</item>
<item>
<title>Alza začala prodávat počítače za 17 milionů. Netradičně jsou skladem a lze si je hned odvézt</title>
<link>https://www.lupa.cz/aktuality/alza-zacala-prodavat-pocitace-za-17-milionu-netradicne-jsou-skladem-a-lze-si-je-hned-odvezt/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=text&utm_campaign=rss</link>
<description>Největ&#353;í tuzemský internetový obchod Alza.cz naskladnil servery pro umělou inteligenci. Ty si tak lze rychle koupit, vyzvednout, případně si je nechat dovézt. Zní to jako banalita, ale tak jednoduché to není. AI infrastruktura je, podobně jako běžný serverový hardware, dlouhodobě nedostupná a čekací doby jsou často velmi dlouhé. Poptávka je stále masivní, což drží nahoře ceny pamětí, hardwaru a elektroniky.</description>

<author>redakce@lupa.cz (Lupa.cz: Jan Sedlák)</author>
<pubDate>Tue, 13 Oct 2026 09:36:17 GMT</pubDate>

<description>České Radiokomunikace (CRA) od leto&#353;ního listopadu reorganizují svůj stále rostoucí a důležitěj&#353;í byznys s datovými centry, cloudem a provozem serverů. Z CRA budou prvního listopadu vyčleněna aktiva do dvou nástupnických firem, kterými budou Datové centrum Lužice a Cloud4com. CRA jsou v obou jediným akcionářem.</description>

<title>Krabicovým hrám odzvonilo. Legendární český e-shop otočil kormidlo a hlásí rekordní čísla</title>
<link>https://www.lupa.cz/aktuality/krabicovym-hram-odzvonilo-legendarni-cesky-e-shop-otocil-kormidlo-a-hlasi-rekordni-cisla/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=text&utm_campaign=rss</link>
<description>Českému internetovému obchodu Xzone se podařil velký obrat. Firma před lety vznikla jako e-shop specializovaný na hry, konzole a příslu&#353;enství kolem. Prodeje krabicových verzí her ov&#353;em s nástupem digitální distribuce typu Steam nebo PlayStation Network ustoupily do pozadí. Xzone zareagovalo příklonem k merchandisingu, oblečení, deskovkám a dal&#353;ímu popkulturnímu sortimentu, což zafungovalo.</description>

<item>
<title>Třetina dospělých už řešila s AI svou psychickou krizi, stát nyní chce řešit, jak téma pojmout</title>
<link>https://www.lupa.cz/aktuality/tretina-dospelych-uz-resila-s-ai-svou-psychickou-krizi-stat-nyni-chce-resit-jak-tema-pojmout/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=text&utm_campaign=rss</link>
<description>Lidé se stále častěji obracejí na umělou inteligenci i s problémy, které se týkají jejich psychiky. Podle jarního výzkumu ji v souvislosti s du&#353;evním zdravím během předchozích 30 dnů použila víc než polovina lidí ve věku 18 až 34 let. Téměř třetina uživatelů s ní už ře&#353;ila psychickou krizi nebo akutní stres. A podobný podíl ji alespoň někdy využil místo odborné pomoci. Ministerstvo zdravotnictví proto při&#353;lo s oznámením, že chystá doporučení, jak AI při ře&#353;ení psychických potíží bezpečně používat. Téma začlenilo i do národního akčního plánu.</description>

<author>redakce@lupa.cz (Lupa.cz: Iva Brejlová)</author>
<pubDate>Tue, 13 Oct 2026 11:20:52 GMT</pubDate>
<enclosure url="https://i.iinfo.cz/images/329/umela-inteligence-ai-1.jpg" length='19538' type="image/jpeg"/>
<guid isPermaLink="false">www.lupa.cz-actuality-18548</guid>


</item>
<item>
<title>Alza začala prodávat počítače za 17 milionů. Netradičně jsou skladem a lze si je hned odvézt</title>
<link>https://www.lupa.cz/aktuality/alza-zacala-prodavat-pocitace-za-17-milionu-netradicne-jsou-skladem-a-lze-si-je-hned-odvezt/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=text&utm_campaign=rss</link>
<description>Největ&#353;í tuzemský internetový obchod Alza.cz naskladnil servery pro umělou inteligenci. Ty si tak lze rychle koupit, vyzvednout, případně si je nechat dovézt. Zní to jako banalita, ale tak jednoduché to není. AI infrastruktura je, podobně jako běžný serverový hardware, dlouhodobě nedostupná a čekací doby jsou často velmi dlouhé. Poptávka je stále masivní, což drží nahoře ceny pamětí, hardwaru a elektroniky.</description>

Kudy z nudy – Žebříčky: Liberecký kraj Žebříčky RSS Feed <![CDATA[Šťastné a křišťálové – Vánoce naruby]]>

Přijďte prožít advent do libereckého Paláce Liebieg, kde se letos potkají tradice, kreativita a vánoční atmosféra Křišťálového údolí. Čeká vás jedinečná výstava, která vás zavede do světa fantazie, kde nic není takové, jak se na první pohled zdá.

]]> Fri, 09 Oct 2026 15:54:49 GMT <![CDATA[Židovská modlitebna a synagoga Liberec]]>

Novodobá liberecká synagoga je součástí Krajské vědecké knihovny, známé jako Stavba smíření. Otevřena byla roku 2000 na místě synagogy vypálené nacisty. Trojúhelníkový půdorys připomíná část Davidovy hvězdy a interiér uchovává památky původního svatostánku.

]]> Fri, 09 Oct 2026 11:36:28 GMT <![CDATA[Kostel sv. Vojtěcha v Liberci]]>

Kostel sv. Vojtěcha v libereckém Ostašově stojí na místě dřevěné kaple vybudované z odškodnění za sedmiletou válku. Zděná stavba vznikla v letech 1832–1833. Díky péči Spolku přátel Ostašova dnes ožívá koncerty a dalšími kulturními akcemi.

]]> Fri, 09 Oct 2026 11:29:30 GMT <![CDATA[Kostel sv. Jana Křtitele v Liberci]]>

Barokní kostel sv. Jana Křtitele v liberecké Rochlici stojí na místě někdejšího dřevěného evangelického kostela. Zaujme dochovaným historickým vybavením, hlavním oltářem s obrazem patrona chrámu, vyřezávanou kazatelnou a varhanami z roku 1887.

]]> Fri, 09 Oct 2026 11:23:32 GMT

Alkohol byl u obou vyloučen.</description></item><item><title>Příprava na zimu na Ještědu začíná: Unikátní technologie chrlí tuny ledu denně</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/902811-priprava-na-zimu-na-jestedu-zacina-unikatni-technologie-chrli-tuny-ledu-denne.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/902811-priprava-na-zimu-na-jestedu-zacina-unikatni-technologie-chrli-tuny-ledu-denne.html</guid><pubDate>Mon, 12 Oct 2026 18:00:00 +0200</pubDate><dc:creator>Martina Petrášková</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>Skiareál Ještěd se intenzivně připravuje na zimní sezónu a znovu sází na technologii Snow Factory. Ta dokáže vyrobit až 96 tun ledu denně zcela bez ohledu na venkovní teplotu. Unikátní metoda bez použití chemie vytvoří pevný základ na kritických úsecích sjezdovek a výrazně urychlí zahájení lyžování.</description></item><item><title>Proč nesmí děti cestovat v bundě? Tohle se stane při nehodě</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/doprava/902440-proc-nesmi-deti-cestovat-v-bunde-tohle-se-stane-pri-nehode.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/doprava/902440-proc-nesmi-deti-cestovat-v-bunde-tohle-se-stane-pri-nehode.html</guid><pubDate>Mon, 12 Oct 2026 16:41:00 +0200</pubDate><category>Doprava</category><description>Péřovka v autosedačce může být při nehodě stejně nebezpečná jako nezapnutý pás. S prvními mrazy se do aut vrací péřové bundy a kombinézy – a s nimi i častý problém: pás autosedačky přes tlustou vrstvu oblečení nezajistí dítě tak, jak má.</description></item><item><title>Neúčast v koalici v Liberci je pro ANO zklamáním, v opozici bude po 12 letech</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/politika/902798-neucast-v-koalici-v-liberci-je-pro-ano-zklamanim-v-opozici-bude-po-12.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/politika/902798-neucast-v-koalici-v-liberci-je-pro-ano-zklamanim-v-opozici-bude-po-12.html</guid><pubDate>Mon, 12 Oct 2026 15:00:00 +0200</pubDate><dc:creator>ČTK</dc:creator><category>Politika</category><description>Neúčast v radniční koalici v Liberci je pro ANO zklamáním. Hnutí o zapojení do koalice usilovalo, řekl lídr ANO Tomáš Rec ČTK. Součástí vedení Liberce bylo ANO posledních 12 let, i když v každém z uplynulých tří volebních období do něj vyslalo jiné zástupce.</description></item></channel></rss>
